digest.intro: War crimes, cloud wreckage, and 2,000-year-old ink lit up like a Christmas tree.

items.title: UN finds reasonable grounds US committed war crimes in Iran school strike
items.blurb: A UN fact-finding mission concluded a US Tomahawk missile collapsed the roof of Shajareh Tayyebeh primary school in Minab on February 28, killing 156 civilians including 120 children — a building they describe as 'clearly identifiable.' The Pentagon's own investigation reportedly concluded months ago; its findings remain classified, while senior commanders are said to have been warned that targeting data was dangerously outdated before the strike.

items.title: Iran strikes permanently destroyed AWS data across an entire region
items.blurb: Iranian drone strikes on Amazon data centers in Bahrain wiped out data across all three availability zones — exceeding what AWS's own multi-AZ redundancy architecture was designed to survive. The destruction represents the first real test of hyperscale cloud infrastructure under kinetic warfare, and the answer is: it failed at a scale the system wasn't designed to contemplate.

items.title: Middle powers are playing every board simultaneously
items.blurb: With BRICS (now 10 full members, 10 partner countries) and UNGA both convening this month, countries like Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan are running parallel strategies — signing a new Mecca defense pact while simultaneously pushing for UN reforms. The clearest signal of the post-US-hegemony moment: middle powers aren't choosing sides, they're joining everything at once.

items.title: California's net neutrality law traded away for broadband cash
items.blurb: The Trump NTIA is making $1.86 billion in BEAD broadband grants conditional on California agreeing not to enforce its net neutrality law — not just in funded areas, but statewide, for up to 14 years. California won a lengthy court battle to defend that law; now it's being circumvented not through litigation but through the leverage of infrastructure money.

items.title: Researchers burned their own scrolls to decode Herculaneum's lead-ink papyri
items.blurb: To figure out which of the 2,000-year-old Herculaneum scrolls are worth digitally unwrapping, researchers deliberately charred replica papyrus rolls and ran them through CT scanners — repurposing software originally designed for lithium-ion battery analysis — and found that lead-based ink lights up in X-ray 'like a Christmas tree.' The double move of destroying copies to preserve originals, using battery-industry imaging tools to read ancient philosophy, is exactly the kind of unreasonable cross-domain obsession that actually moves archaeology forward.

items.title: How SpaceX went from a tangle of pipes to the Raptor 3
items.blurb: Brian Potter traces how SpaceX reduced the Raptor from a rat's nest of external plumbing to a smooth, almost featureless cylinder — achieving 35% more thrust in the process — by internalizing routing, eliminating intermediate fittings, and designing manufacturing constraints into the geometry from the start. The rival CEO who called the Raptor 3 photos 'exaggerated' because no assembled engine could look like that is a good measure of how far outside normal aerospace reasoning this work sits.

items.title: The cryptographic infrastructure behind every US driver's license barcode was recoverable
items.blurb: Ryan Fahey reverse-engineered and recovered the signing keys used to verify US state ID barcodes — infrastructure that underlies identity checks at bars, airports, and dispensaries across the country. The systemic failure isn't just one state's bad key hygiene; it's a story about what happens when critical verification systems get built without anyone treating the cryptographic root of trust as the thing that actually needs protecting.

items.title: Hew Locke's flotilla of colonial ghosts
items.blurb: Locke's new show at P·P·O·W suspends a fleet of miniature ships from the gallery ceiling — galleons alongside tankers, all adorned with pennants and foliage — as a single argument about how empire's economic logic doesn't end, it just changes vessels. The busts of Victoria and Washington draped in glittering baubles, rendered in Parian ware (19th-century cheap marble substitute), add another layer: prestige materials imitating prestige, all the way down.

items.title: Fake marble: 2,000 years of humans desperately wanting the real thing
items.blurb: Aeon's essay-film tracks the continuous thread from Roman fresco painters imitating stone grain to modern kitchen countertop laminates — asking what it means that simulation of a prestige surface has itself become a prestige tradition. The obsession is never really about marble; it's about what surfaces are allowed to signal and who gets to use them.

items.title: Who will taste the cherries if computers count all the petals?
items.blurb: Starting from a Silicon Valley test kitchen building an oven designed to produce Michelin-quality food at a button press, this essay excavates the 'computist dream' — the centuries-long project of debugging subjectivity out of human knowledge until experience becomes pure frictionless data. The question it won't let go of: when a system can optimize every measurable quality of a dish, what exactly is the taster for?

facts.fact: AWS's Bahrain region lost data across all three availability zones — meaning Iran's strikes exceeded the maximum failure scenario the platform was architecturally designed to survive.
The Raptor 3 produces about 35% more thrust than the Raptor 1, while looking — from the outside — like almost a completely different object with most of its plumbing hidden internally.

Researchers studying Herculaneum scrolls found that lead-based ancient ink illuminates so brightly under X-ray CT that they described it as lighting up 'like a Christmas tree' — making those scrolls the highest-priority targets for digital unwrapping.
California's BEAD broadband grant agreement would exempt ISPs from the state's net neutrality law not just in areas receiving funding, but statewide, for up to 14 years.

The UN fact-finding mission found that the Minab school struck on February 28 was 'clearly identifiable' as a school — a key threshold in war crimes law distinguishing lawful military targets from protected civilian sites.

art_picks.title: Leviathan
art_picks.creator: Lucien Castaing-Taylor & Véréna Paravel (Sensory Ethnography Lab)
art_picks.why: A 2012 documentary shot with cameras lashed to fishing nets, hooks, and deckhands — the physical/digital edge at its most visceral. No narration, no arc, just the system of a commercial fishing boat rendered as pure sensation. The kind of obsessive formal commitment that makes you want to rethink every creative constraint you have.

art_picks.title: The Clock
art_picks.creator: Christian Marclay
art_picks.why: A 24-hour film collage that syncs cinema time to real time — tens of thousands of clock moments edited into an instrument that actually tells the hour. It's systems thinking as art, a feedback loop between collective cultural memory and lived present. Obsessive craft at an almost incomprehensible scale, and the experience of watching it shifts how you feel inside your own day.

art_picks.title: Replica
art_picks.creator: Oneohtrix Point Never
art_picks.why: Daniel Lopatin built this 2011 record entirely from TV commercial samples — jingles, soundbites, product voice-overs — dissolved into ambient drift until the source is unrecognizable. It's an archaeology of consumer culture that sounds like beautiful ruins; the invisible system (late-capitalist media) becomes emotionally raw through formal transformation.

events.name: Camille Henrot: Dogs
events.venue: Doris C. Freedman Plaza, Central Park (Public Art Fund)
events.why: Henrot's first NYC public commission — a group of handcrafted dog sculptures that are, characteristically, never just what they look like: dogs as symbols of domesticity, control, and the human need to make wildness legible; free, outdoors, and right there if you're in the park.

events.name: Brice Marden Survey
events.why: A comprehensive career survey — six decades of paintings, the first show of his work in New York in twenty years, with major loans from the Art Institute of Chicago and the Whitney; Marden's slow, embodied mark-making is the opposite of algorithmic art and hits hard right now for that reason.

events.name: Clio Art Fair — 'I Don't Want to Be Useful'
events.why: Self-representing artists only, no gallery intermediaries, organized around an 'anti-fair' ethos and a theme of optimistic nihilism — includes a performance art program; small, weird, and direct in exactly the ways the Armory isn't.

events.name: SPRING/BREAK Art Show — 'Hide N Seek' (15th Edition)
events.why: The curator-driven anti-fair that takes over raw, atypical spaces — 100+ independent curatorial projects organized around encoding, concealment, and symbolic language; consistently the most formally adventurous fair week event, and the antidote to booth-style art fair fatigue.

events.name: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony
events.why: Jafa's largest-ever survey — forty years of film, montage, painting, and sculpture that treats images as 'fugitive, virulent cultural agents,' mining internet culture and Black popular music to interrogate how identity is constructed, commodified, and consumed; opens during the window and is immediately the most important show in the city.
